docs.title: Lecture 4 · Why Independent Validation Is Needed: Pre-Registration and the Validation Pipeline
docs.text: Chapter 2 · Honest Validation (Lecture 1) Learning objectives: understand the institutional difference between "factory self-reported results" and "independent validation"; master core concepts such as pre-registration, DSR, and the one-shot out-of-sample verdict. Prerequisite: Chapter 1 (especially Lecture 2's "three must-ask questions").

docs.title: 1. Starting from One Number
docs.text:
Chapter 1 ended with a number: 290 factors, top self-reported excess +26.5%, zero survivors under independent validation. This lecture answers: what exactly is "independent validation" independent of, and why are its conclusions more credible than the factory's numbers?

First, a comparison. The factory backtest and independent validation do similar things — both compute factor returns on historical data. The difference is not in compute or code quality, but in institutions:

Dimension Factory built-in backtest Independent validation pipeline Data Campaign panel (the same copy) Independently pulled, independently cleaned recomputation panel Rules Can be adjusted while watching results (the loop is naturally so) Pre-registered: decision rules written down and archived first Verdict A leaderboard ranking, no threshold One-shot verdict: threshold pre-registered; once triggered, it is final Target Every factor gets a number Only the very few candidates passing initial screening Nature of conclusion Descriptive ("how much did it return") Adjudicative ("reject/inconclusive/support")

In one sentence: the factory backtest answers "what would happen if we used it"; independent validation answers "is it actually real". The former is description; the latter is a statistical verdict.

docs.title: 2. Multiple Testing: Why "Adjust While Watching" Necessarily Produces False Positives
docs.text:
This is the first principle of all validation science, worth spelling out slowly.

Suppose all 290 factors are pure noise (zero correlation with future returns). Testing each factor at the 5% significance level, you expect 290 × 0.05 ≈ 14.5 "significantly effective" factors. These 14.5 look exactly like real factors on the leaderboard — significance does not write "I am luck" on your face.

This problem already existed in manual human research (academia calls it a breeding ground for p-hacking); the LLM loop scaled up the base by two orders of magnitude and dropped the cost to zero — so multiple testing went from "a bias to watch out for" to "the system's dominant failure mode".

The only institutional countermeasure is pre-registration:

  1. Before looking at the data, write down and archive: the candidate factor list, the validation data window, the decision thresholds, the statistical conventions, and "what to do if inconclusive"
  2. At validation time, execute strictly per the archive; post-hoc adjustment of any rule is forbidden
  3. A rule change = a change of experiment identity = the whole thing must be rerun, and the old conclusion is void

The essence of pre-registration is not ceremony but locking down the researcher degrees of freedom before the results come out. The "parameter-tunable overlay factor" you met in Lecture 2 consumes degrees of freedom inside the factor; "deciding which benchmark, which window, which threshold after seeing results" consumes degrees of freedom at the validation stage — the latter is more hidden and more lethal.

docs.title: 3. The Four Components of the Validation Pipeline
docs.text: Using the real pipeline that accompanies this course (AIResearchPlatform, separate storage from the factory, independent data pulls):

docs.title: Component one: independent data recomputation
docs.text: The validation panel is not copied from the campaign panel but independently pulled and recomputed from the data source. The reason comes straight from practice: the double-adjustment bug behind the carry factor's +18% hid in the campaign panel's construction code — if validation had directly consumed that panel, the bug would have been inherited as-is and the correction would never have happened. (The dedicated chapter on convention issues is Chapter 3.)

docs.title: Component two: pre-registered thresholds
docs.text:
Example thresholds used in the real campaign (written into the pre-registration document before any OOS data could be touched):

  • DSR (Deflated Sharpe Ratio): a multiple-testing correction on the Sharpe — you tried N strategies, so the significance threshold must rise accordingly. The larger N, the higher the bar, and the harder for the top name to clear it
  • Primary/secondary referees: besides the primary criterion, a secondary criterion with a different convention (e.g., price convention vs funding-rate convention); when the two disagree, "supported" may not be declared
  • Per-year constraint: a structure of "all returns come from one year" is disallowed — a single year's contribution above the cap is vetoed, preventing one market episode from being mistaken for a law
  • Orthogonalization opponents: a candidate must retain residual alpha after orthogonalizing against known style factors (momentum, value, low-vol, liquidity); whatever is explained by existing factors does not count as a new discovery

docs.title: Component three: the one-shot out-of-sample verdict (OOS one-shot)
docs.text:
Out-of-sample data is a consumable: each use contaminates it once. The rule is that one OOS window permits exactly one verdict —

  • SUPPORTED: advance to the next stage (shadow monitoring, Chapter 4)
  • REJECTED: archive the conclusion; that hypothesis family goes on the "no re-test" list (preventing another shot at the OOS in a different costume)
  • INCONCLUSIVE (e.g., insufficient power): freeze; you may only wait for new forward data or a new pre-registration; lowering the threshold and retrying is forbidden

docs.title: Component four: paper trail and reproducibility
docs.text: Validation reports are archived on disk (data fingerprints, code versions, threshold values), recomputable by anyone at any time. This is not just scientific norms but also insurance for your future self — Lecture 9 will show that several major errata (including the +18% fake carry) were discovered and corrected precisely because "historical conclusions can be recomputed".

docs.title: 4. Three Real Verdicts from One-Shot Decisions
docs.text:
The three outcomes this institution produces each have real cases, forming the next two lectures:

Verdict Case Numbers Lecture REJECTED Earnings forecast event window OOS spread −0.49% (direction reversed), discovery period also ineffective Lecture 6 INCONCLUSIVE Index rebalancing flow OOS +1.00%, p=0.062 — insufficient power, frozen Lecture 6 SUPPORTED crypto funding carry OOS +2.37%/yr, p<0.0001, passed all eight sub-checks Chapter 4

Note the relative magnitudes of the three numbers: the only surviving strategy annualizes 2.37%; the two rejected ones had far more dazzling discovery-period numbers. Real alpha is small and ugly; fake alpha is big and plausible — this is not a coincidence but a structural feature of this industry, and every later lecture returns to it.

docs.title: 5. Lecture Summary
docs.text:
• The factory backtest is description; independent validation is verdict; the difference is institutional, not computational
  • Multiple testing is the loop-mining's dominant failure mode; pre-registration is the only institutional antidote
  • Four pipeline components: independent data, pre-registered thresholds (DSR/primary-secondary referees/per-year/orthogonalization opponents), one-shot OOS verdict, reproducible paper trail
  • Each verdict has a real case: REJECTED (−0.49%), INCONCLUSIVE (+1.00%, p=0.062), SUPPORTED (+2.37%/yr)

Discussion question: A colleague says "the DSR threshold is too strict — none of our 290 factors can pass; let's loosen it to the 10% significance level". Point out the two logical errors in that statement. (Hints: what does a threshold control? What does changing the threshold amount to?)

docs.title: Lecture 5 · Three Candidates All FAIL DSR: Where the Excess Came From, and Where It Went
docs.text: Chapter 2 · Honest Validation (Lecture 2) Learning objectives: through the complete retrospective of the A-share campaign, understand the concrete mechanics of "leaderboard looks great → independent validation wipes them all out". Prerequisite: Lecture 4.

docs.title: 1. Case Background
docs.text:
After the A-share campaign (2026-09-18~22) ended, three top candidates were selected from the 290-factor leaderboard via the pre-registered process and sent into the independent validation pipeline. The verdict:

All three candidates FAIL DSR.

This lecture's task is to unpack the words "all FAIL": where each candidate's excess appeared to come from, where it actually came from, and under which blade it died at validation.

docs.title: 2. The First Blade: DSR — You Pay Back as Many Tries as You Made
docs.text:
Recall Lecture 4: DSR corrects the Sharpe for the number of trials N. The three candidates came from the top of a 290-factor leaderboard, so N is not 3 but 290 (strictly it should also count each factor's multiple evaluations — Lecture 2 showed a single factor, momentum_20d, had 23 evaluations; total evaluations across the pool number in the thousands).

A back-of-envelope: even if a candidate's raw Sharpe were significant in the "single test" sense, after correction for a trial base in the thousands, the required threshold is pushed to a level ordinary numbers can essentially never reach. This is not a harsh threshold; it is simply the fact — the best outcome picked out of a thousand coin flips should not be judged by the standard of a single flip.

All three candidates fell at this gate. Note this blade's kill logic: it does not say "these three factors are necessarily invalid"; it says "these three, having survived a thousand-way selection, have results insufficient to prove they are not luck". Evidence insufficient — treated as the inverse of the presumption of innocence: not admitted.

docs.title: 3. The Second Blade: Attribution Decomposition — Is the Excess Alpha or Style Beta
docs.text:
The second thing the validation pipeline did to the candidates: an orthogonalization test (regress on known style factors, look at the residual). The campaign's portfolio-level attribution was even more extreme:

The equal-weight composite portfolio had OOS IC 0.043, seemingly effective; but after orthogonalizing against three known styles — industry + low-vol + liquidity — 92% of the return was explained away, and the residual alpha's t-stat = 0.14.

Translated into plain language: the money this "AI factor portfolio" made, 92% of it can be replicated by "buying a pile of low-volatility, high-liquidity stocks with a skewed industry distribution" — all three things known for decades, no need for an AI to compute hundreds of factors overnight. The true residual portion, t=0.14, is statistically zero.

This is the leaderboard's favorite magic trick: packaging style beta as alpha and selling it to you. The leaderboard doesn't care whether you earned new money — the excess return column does not distinguish "discovering something nobody else knew" from "being heavily loaded on a known style". And for the latter you can just buy a low-vol ETF, without paying the cost of factor mining.

docs.title: 4. The Third Blade: Turnover and Cost — Gross Return Cannot Buy Back Net Return
docs.text:
Lecture 3 planted the thread: the momentum family with 33 versions is the hardest hit by turnover. The validation pipeline recomputed on a net-of-cost basis: with the top candidates' turnover levels (campaign-measured around 40%+ two-sided per rebalance period) plus A-share trading costs, the gross excess was eroded to insignificance on a net basis.

The leaderboard shows gross or semi-net numbers (the second of Lecture 2's "three must-ask questions"). The factory has no incentive to show net numbers — it doesn't know your fee schedule, and moreover net numbers would make the leaderboard ugly.

docs.title: 5. The Deepest Blade: The Benchmark Artifact (Preview of Lecture 8)
docs.text:
During the three candidates' validation, an even more fundamental problem was discovered: the benchmark itself had a convention flaw (under the CSI 300 convention, limit-up stocks were excluded), so a chunk of the "excess" was an artifact created by the benchmark's definition. Recomputed with the honest convention, the biweekly top200 portfolio had no excess at all.

What makes this discovery stunning is its layer: it is not at the layer of "is the factor good" but at the layer of "is the quantity 'excess' itself trustworthy". However rigorous factor validation is, if the benchmark is wrong, the foundation of every conclusion is wrong. The full treatment is left for Lecture 8 — here you only need to remember the shape of the lesson: validation must dig down to the data foundation, not stop at the factor layer.

docs.title: 6. Retrospective: The Layered Structure of the Four Blades
docs.text:
Stack the four blades and you see they form a bottom-up audit stack:

第 4 层  统计充分性   DSR / 多重检验校正     —— 成绩配得上选拔基数吗
第 3 层  收益来源     正交化 / 归因分解      —— 是新钱还是旧 beta
第 2 层  可实现性     换手 × 成本敏感性      —— 净费后还在吗
第 1 层  数据地基     基准口径 / 面板构建    —— 量本身可不可信

The factory's leaderboard operates only below layer 4, and does only half of it (no correction). The value of independent validation is walking the full stack — the three candidates took one blade at each of the four layers, and none died because "the factor's logic itself was falsified"; all died of insufficient evidence and flawed conventions. This is precisely Lecture 4's sentence in the flesh: validation judges "is it real", not "how good is it".

docs.title: 7. The Morale Problem: What to Do After All FAIL
docs.text:
After a total wipeout there are two natural emotional reactions, both to be resisted:

  • "Validation is too strict; loosen the thresholds" — loosening thresholds = re-introducing multiple testing. The all-FAIL conclusion was always "insufficient evidence"; loosening the standard does not make evidence sufficient, it only lets false positives in the door.
  • "AI factor mining is useless; abandon it" — an overreaction. The correct reading: the AI factory's value proposition needs restating. Its qualified output is not "factors ready to deploy" but "a stream of candidate hypotheses generated at low cost". Between the candidate stream and a deployable strategy lies an entire validation pipeline — that pipeline always existed for human researchers too (peer review + small live-money trial and error); it was just never formally built as part of the production process.

The campaign's actual decision was a third path: keep the factory, formally build the validation institution, archive "zero excess under the honest convention" as-is — and then pivot. The first pre-registered experiment after the pivot (Lecture 6) and the only surviving strategy (Chapter 4) were both born after this institution was established.

docs.title: 8. Lecture Summary
docs.text:
• The three candidates' causes of death, four layers: DSR (thousand-way selection base), style beta posing as alpha (92% explained, residual t=0.14), net-cost erosion, benchmark artifact
  • The leaderboard's magic: doesn't distinguish new money from old beta, shows gross returns, applies no selection correction
  • The correct reading of all-FAIL: the AI factory's unit of output is a "candidate hypothesis stream", not "deployable factors"
  • The four-layer audit stack: statistical sufficiency → return source → realizability → data foundation; miss a layer and killers can slip through

Discussion question: Suppose a candidate passes DSR and orthogonalization, but its net-of-cost excess is exactly zero (gross excess = costs). Would you judge SUPPORTED, REJECTED, or INCONCLUSIVE? Give your reasoning. (No standard answer — the real campaign's ruling checked items one by one against the threshold table in the pre-registration; the point of this question is to think about "whether your threshold table has this cell".)

docs.title: Lecture 6 · The Full Lifecycle of One Pre-Registered Experiment: Two Verdicts
docs.text: Chapter 2 · Honest Validation (Lecture 3, chapter finale) Learning objectives: follow two real hypotheses from project initiation to verdict, mastering the operational details of a pre-registered experiment and the boundaries between the three verdicts. Prerequisites: Lectures 4 and 5.

docs.title: 1. Why These Two Cases
docs.text: Lecture 5's all-FAIL was the fate of "batch candidates"; this lecture follows the full lifecycle of individual hypotheses — a human proposes an idea, writes the pre-registration, walks through validation, receives the verdict, and executes the verdict's consequences. The two cases, one REJECTED and one INCONCLUSIVE, exactly cover the two hardest operations: "what to do after a rejection" and "what to do when evidence is insufficient". (The SUPPORTED case is left for Chapter 4, to avoid structurally arriving at a happy ending too early.)

docs.title: 2. Case One: Earnings Forecast Event Window — REJECTED
2.1 Hypothesis
docs.text: Around A-share earnings forecast disclosures there is a tradable mispricing window: stocks whose forecasts beat expectations continue to drift for several days after the event (a forecast version of post-earnings announcement drift, PEAD). Data basis: the earnings forecast (forecast) + former-name-change (namechange) panels.

docs.title: 2.2 Pre-registration essentials
docs.text: Elements locked before the verdict (excerpt): event window definition, control group construction, OOS window, spread threshold (direction + magnitude + significance), and the boundaries of the three verdicts. Archived before touching any OOS data.

docs.title: 2.3 Verdict
docs.text:
OOS spread −0.49%, direction reversed. REJECTED, one-shot verdict.

The discovery period (IS segment) likewise showed no usable positive spread — this detail matters: it is not the classic overfitting shape of "effective in discovery, fails out of sample"; it never existed from beginning to end. The hypothesis itself was wrong, not unlucky data.

docs.title: 2.4 Executing the Verdict — Where the Institution Shows Its Mettle
docs.text:
After REJECTED landed, three things happened, each worth telling:

  1. Hypothesis family ban: the event-window family of hypotheses entered the "no re-test" list — no applying for another OOS with a different window definition or control construction. The same OOS window is a consumable, and it was already spent on this question.
  2. Data asset retention: the forecast + namechange panels were stored as reusable assets. What was rejected is the hypothesis, not the data — data has no side; other hypotheses can use it later.
  3. Incidental observations downgraded: along the way a hint of "post-forecast reversal" was noticed, but since it was not pre-registered and is a variant within the hypothesis family, it was flagged as hypothesis-generating (generates hypotheses only, constitutes no evidence) and forbidden from entering the next validation round directly. To pursue it, write a new pre-registration first.

Item 3 is the most subtle and the most frequently violated: "while validating A I happened to notice B seems to work" — that "noticing" itself has already consumed one look at the data. The institutionally correct handling is not to pretend you didn't see it, but to downgrade it to a hypothesis and run the full process again. What you noticed in passing is not evidence; it is a lead.

docs.title: 3. Case Two: Index Rebalancing Flow — INCONCLUSIVE
3.1 Hypothesis
docs.text: When an index periodically rebalances, passive funds buy and sell in bulk per the announced list, creating predictable short-term price pressure (the inflow/outflow flow between the rebalancing announcement date and the effective date). This is a phenomenon with literature precedent (index rebalancing effect), one prior tier above AI-generated overlay factors (Lecture 3's conclusion two applies here).

docs.title: 3.2 Process and Assembly Validation
docs.text: This case adds a real engineering step: assembly testing. The rebalancing-flow strategy's input is an assembly pipeline of "announced list → passive AUM estimate → flow direction sign"; any misalignment (dates, direction, weights) silently produces garbage. The assembly pipeline first passed a PASS check (sampling the assembled output against the announcement text), and only then entered pre-registration. Validate the data pipeline first, then the strategy hypothesis — the order cannot be reversed.

docs.title: 3.3 Verdict
docs.text: Discovery period +0.95%; OOS +1.00%, p = 0.062. INCONCLUSIVE — insufficient power, frozen.

docs.title: 3.4 The Correct Handling of INCONCLUSIVE (Harder than REJECTED)
docs.text:
REJECTED is quick and clean; INCONCLUSIVE tortures you — a p-value 0.038 short, and human nature screams "try again". The rules:

  • Freeze; no re-test with changed conventions: extending the window a year, switching the statistical test, dropping a month — every one of these is "adjusting rules after seeing results", exactly the researcher degrees of freedom Lecture 4 locked down
  • No declaring "essentially effective": the external vocabulary has exactly three words; INCONCLUSIVE means it may not appear in any report's "effective strategies" column
  • Only two ways out: wait for new forward data to accumulate (time for power), or write a new pre-registration for a forward round (register the thresholds before the next real rebalancing occurs, and judge with data that has not yet happened)

The case's actual disposition: OOS frozen, with a subsequent re-pre-registration on the forward route (the 2026-12 rebalancing round is within forward monitoring coverage). "Waiting" is also part of the verdict — accepting that "this question cannot be answered now" is the most anti-human and most money-saving rule in multiple-testing discipline.

docs.title: 4. The Decision Tree of Three Verdicts (Chapter Wrap-Up)
docs.text:
Stacking all cases from Lecture 4 through this lecture into one adjudication cheat sheet:

预注册验证结果
├─ 过全部门槛（DSR/副判据/分年/净费/正交）
│    → SUPPORTED → 影子监控 30 天（第四章）→ 部署决策
├─ 方向反 / 分年结构违规 / 正交后无残差
│    → REJECTED → 假设族封禁，数据保留，衍生观察降级
└─ 方向对但功效不足（p 略高、窗口短）
     → INCONCLUSIVE → 冻结：等前向数据 or 新预注册前向轮
                          （禁止：改门槛、改口径、原窗重测）

Note there is no edge in the tree leading to "close enough, deploy a small position first". Position size is not a substitute for validation — probing an unadjudicated hypothesis with real money is running a non-reproducible experiment at maximum cost.

docs.title: 5. Chapter 2 Summary
docs.text:
• Independent validation = institution, not compute: pre-registration locks down degrees of freedom, DSR corrects the selection base, one-shot OOS verdicts
  • The fate of batch candidates (Lecture 5): wiped out across the four-layer audit stack; the AI factory's qualified output is a candidate hypothesis stream
  • The fate of single hypotheses (this lecture): REJECTED bans the family and keeps the data, INCONCLUSIVE freezes and waits for forward data — a verdict's value lies in its execution
  • The only surviving case annualizes just 2.37%: real alpha is small and ugly; fake alpha is big and plausible

Chapter 2 demonstrated that "honest validation" can be executed as an institution. Chapter 3 turns to its foundation: when the data itself is broken, even the strictest validation gets silently contaminated — double adjustment, benchmark artifacts, misaligned date stamps: five real data mines.

docs.title: Chapter 3 · Hidden Mines in Data Conventions
docs.text:
Lecture notes for Chapter 3 (Lectures 7–9) of "When AI Mines Factors, How Not to Be Fooled — by Yourself or by the AI". Theme: the foundation audit beneath the validation institution — data construction, the definition of quantities, convention agreements.

Lecture File Topic Core case 7 E07_双重复权.md Adjustment mechanics, plausibility bias, the four-piece erratum downstream carry +18% → +3.18% (t=0.66), D-9 8 E08_基准伪影.md Benchmark degrees of freedom, quantity-definition-layer audit, differences vs levels Benchmark excludes-limit-up artifact; dividend double deduction (1+r)/f_ratio² 9 E09_期货面板五坑.md Six-step convention audit process, five failure types Night-session date stamps / roll gaps / $oi erratum / end-of-panel overrun

docs.title: Data facts for this chapter (sources for reference)
docs.text:
• D-9 erratum (2026-10-01): carry discovery-period +18% was double adjustment; after correction +3.18%, t=0.66; protocol versioned as v1.0+D-9 revision; power withdrawal (350-day window, normal approximation ~7%); L2 downgraded to a watch line, deployment investment suspended
  • A-share benchmark erratum (2026-09-23): benchmark excluding limit-ups caused an excess artifact; under the honest convention the biweekly top200 had zero excess; excess_honest adopted as the sole convention going forward
  • A-share panel dividend double deduction: true total return = (1+r)/f_ratio², verified with zero error against tushare; relative-quantity conclusions unchanged
  • Futures panel date stamps (2026-09-28): 918 days contained 180 Sunday rows; the vendor stamps by the night session's actual clock time at open; the return series is correct, cross-source joins misalign by one day, returns computed by per-instrument row order
  • Roll detection heuristic: |Δoi| ≥ 30% or open gap |gap| ≥ 3%
  • qlib backtest end calendar[i+1] overrun: the test window's end must precede the panel's last day by ≥1 trading day

docs.title: Lecture 7 · The D-9 Erratum: How an Adjustment Bug Manufactured a Fake 18% Annualized Strategy
docs.text: Chapter 3 · Hidden Mines in Data Conventions (Lecture 1) Learning objectives: understand the adjustment mechanics of futures dominant-continuous contracts and how the "double adjustment" bug arises; master the concept of "plausibility bias"; understand the institutional handling of errata. Prerequisites: Lecture 2 (where the carry factor first appears), Lecture 4 (the pre-registration institution).

docs.title: 1. Case Overview
docs.text:
The futures round-two campaign's research matrix had an L2 line: a term-structure carry strategy (long the deeply discounted instruments, short the ones at premium, earning the spread convergence). The factory's discovery-period backtest gave:

Discovery period annualized +18%, the most dazzling number of the entire campaign, beautiful t-value, reasonable per-year structure.

Nine days later (the erratum event numbered D-9), an audit found a double adjustment in the panel construction. Recomputed after the fix:

Discovery period +3.18%, t = 0.66, statistically indistinguishable from zero.

A number fell from "nearly deployable" to "noise" with only one convention audit in between. The number itself deserves nine days of discussion, but more deserving is: why it nearly fooled everyone — including a validation institution that was already quite strict.

docs.title: 2. Technical Background: Dominant-Continuous Contracts and Adjustment
docs.text:
Futures have no single continuous ticker like stocks. When building a panel, one usually takes the "dominant continuous": each monthly contract expires and switches to the new dominant, and the segments are spliced into one continuous series. At the splice points (roll days) the two contracts have different prices (premium/discount), and splicing directly produces fake gaps — hence adjustment: at roll days, shift or ratio-adjust the historical series as a whole to eliminate the splice gap.

This campaign's panel used settlement-price-splice adjustment: splicing anchored on settlement prices.

The double adjustment bug's mechanism: two places in the construction pipeline each independently adjusted for the roll gap (one an explicit adjustment step, one hidden inside the return series construction). The two adjustments stacked, with the effect of over-correcting slightly in the same direction at every roll. 23 instruments × four years × several rolls per year — the error was not random noise but a systematic one-directional drift.

This is the key: random noise cancels out and makes t-values ugly; systematic bias accumulates in one direction and makes t-values beautiful. The carry strategy naturally holds both long and short legs with holding periods spanning roll days — it swallowed the one-directional drift wholesale into its returns.

docs.title: 3. Why It Nearly Fooled Everyone: Plausibility Bias
docs.text:
This is the concept this lecture most wants to leave you with. Why wasn't the +18% suspected immediately?

Because it looked too reasonable. Term-structure carry has literature precedent (commodity carry is a classic risk premium), and "18% annualized" lands within the expectation band of "this strategy is supposed to make money, and quite a lot of it". The psychological default when humans check numbers is: audit the outrageous, wave through the reasonable — and a high-quality bug produces exactly reasonable numbers.

Contrast with a thought experiment: had the same pipeline error made the carry backtest show annualized −25%, it would not have survived the afternoon — too outrageous, someone would surely investigate. A bug in the wrong direction exposes itself; a bug in the right direction hides itself.

Plausibility bias: the consistency of a number with prior expectations gets misused as evidence of the number's correctness. The two are independent — the bug doesn't understand finance; it just happens to lean the way you hoped.

Corollary: for a result that fits expectations especially well, audit priority should go up, not down. Counterintuitive, but the logic holds: good results get deployed, bad results merely get ignored — being wrong about the good is costly, being wrong about the bad is cheap.

docs.title: 4. How the Erratum Happened: Process, Not Inspiration
docs.text:
This bug was not "spotted"; it was forced out by process. The trigger chain:

  1. Independent recomputation requirement: before the L2 line entered formal validation, the pipeline required the return series to be independently recomputed from raw data, not consuming the factory panel's ready-made return column
  2. Cross-reconciliation: the independent recomputation didn't match the factory panel — the differences concentrated near roll days
  3. Root cause localization: comparing the two code paths, the duplicated adjustment step was found
  4. Erratum execution: panel rebuilt, all historical conclusions restated per "corrected numbers", the erratum document numbered and archived (D-9)

Note step 1 — it is exactly Lecture 4's "component one: independent data recomputation" in the flesh. Had the validation pipeline consumed the factory panel directly, this bug would have been inherited forever, and carry would have marched into shadow monitoring carrying its fake 18% annualized.

The second-order value of the paper trail also shows here: because old conclusions could be recomputed, the erratum could "restate history" rather than "start over" — the +18% was rewritten as +3.18%, not quietly deleted.

docs.title: 5. The Chain of Dispositions After the Erratum (More Important than the Erratum Itself)
docs.text:
Finding the bug is only the beginning; an honest system must handle its entire downstream:

Disposition Content Logic Protocol revision Research protocol versioned (v1.0 + D-9 revision), erratum on record Rule changes must leave a trail, preventing "it changed so it never happened" Power withdrawal The original OOS decision threshold was based on the +18% expected magnitude; after correction, +3.18% corresponds to extremely low statistical power (350-day window, ~7% under normal approximation) — the original threshold effectively cannot adjudicate Thresholds were designed for large effects; after the effect shrinks the threshold fails, and continuing to use it is formalism Priority downgrade L2 demoted from the main line to a low-priority watch line The effect may exist but is too small to justify main-line investment Suspend deployment investment Explicit rule: even if later OOS ≥10%, it does not alone trigger deployment Prevents the "eager to redeem after correction" psychology from re-inflating a small effect Narrow audit annotations Early audit documents annotated with narrowed applicability (rough diagnostics, excluding rolls); historical numbers unchanged An erratum does not tamper with historical documents; it only delimits their scope of validity

"Power withdrawal" deserves the most unpacking: a pre-registered threshold (say, "OOS annualized ≥X% with p<0.05") implicitly assumes the effect size is large enough that the test has adequate power at the available sample size. When the effect shrinks from 18% to 3.18%, the same threshold with the same window can barely ever judge a true effect SUPPORTED. Continuing to run a test with no power yields an uninformative result either way (ACCEPT would be luck; REJECT proves nothing). The honest handling is admitting "this question is undecidable at the current data volume" — exactly the Lecture 6 INCONCLUSIVE verdict recurring in another dimension.

docs.title: 6. Lecture Summary
docs.text:
• Double adjustment = the roll adjustment applied twice; error accumulates systematically in one direction, feeding precisely the carry strategy which holds across rolls
  • Systematic bias makes t-values beautiful; random noise makes them ugly — beautiful numbers are not necessarily cleaner
  • Plausibility bias: the more a result fits expectations, the more easily it passes audit unchallenged; the correction is raising audit priority for expectation-fitting results
  • The four-piece erratum downstream: protocol versioning, power withdrawal, priority downgrade, narrowed historical annotation
  • Independent recomputation is the only institutional means of catching this class of bugs

Discussion question: Suppose the double adjustment bug affected not carry (long/short legs held across rolls) but a 3-day short-horizon reversal strategy (positions never cross a roll day). Would the contamination be heavier or lighter? What audit principle does that suggest? (Hint: the spatial distribution of the bias determines which strategies ingest how much — rank audits by "the contact surface between the strategy and the defect mechanism", not by the strategy's return ranking.)

docs.title: Lecture 8 · Benchmark Artifacts: When the Quantity "Excess" Itself Is Wrong
docs.text: Chapter 3 · Hidden Mines in Data Conventions (Lecture 2) Learning objectives: understand how benchmark conventions systematically manufacture fake excess; master how dividend-handling errors contaminate total returns; build the habit of "auditing down to the quantity-definition layer". Prerequisite: Lecture 5 (where the benchmark artifact is first mentioned).

docs.title: 1. Case Overview
docs.text:
During the A-share campaign's independent validation it was found that in the benchmark construction used by the leaderboard convention, limit-up stocks were excluded. This seemingly harmless detail systematically contaminated the quantity "excess return" itself. Recomputed with the honest convention:

The biweekly-rebalanced top200 portfolio's "excess" over the benchmark vanished entirely. A substantial part of the earlier excess was an artifact created by the benchmark's definition.

Lecture 5 called this the bottommost blade of the four-layer audit stack — however rigorous factor validation is, if the benchmark is wrong, the foundation of every conclusion is wrong. This lecture unfolds that blade in full.

docs.title: 2. Mechanism: How Excluding Limit-Ups Becomes "Excess"
docs.text:
Take the magic trick apart step by step:

Step one: the benchmark contains no limit-up stocks. The benchmark portfolio excluded stocks that hit the daily limit that day (possibly a "tradability" consideration — you can't buy at the limit).

Step two: the strategy portfolio does contain them. The factor's stock-selection logic neither knows nor cares whom the benchmark excluded — strong-momentum stocks and stocks that hit the limit get selected all the same.

Step three: A-share limit-ups have next-day drift. Stocks that hit the limit (especially non-one-board ones) have positive next-day drift on average — a market-microstructure fact (sealing capital, sentiment continuation, the queuing effect under the price-limit system).

Step four: the artifact sets. The strategy portfolio holds a basket containing "next-day positive drift", and the benchmark removed that component — the strategy did nothing right; it merely stood on the opposite side of the benchmark's exclusion rule. The more its picks lean toward limit-ups, the better the "excess" looks. Momentum-type factors (leaderboard heavyweights — recall the 33-version momentum_20d from Lecture 2) are naturally advantaged against a limit-up-excluding benchmark — a sizable chunk of their "alpha" was a gift from that benchmark rule.

Note the toxicity of this artifact: it cannot be arbitraged. Trading this strategy live, you equally cannot buy the limit-up stocks (or you buy at the next day's gap-up open); the backtest "excess" corresponds to fills unavailable in reality. And it is yet another failure mode than Lecture 7's bug — the data isn't wrong, the code isn't wrong, the statistics aren't wrong; the definition of the quantity is guaranteed to mislead.

docs.title: 3. The Hidden Degrees of Freedom in Benchmark Design
docs.text:
This case exposes an often-ignored truth: the benchmark is a research decision with extremely high degrees of freedom, yet it is rarely treated as one. The same history, the same strategy — the benchmark options include:

  • Whole-market equal weight / exclude limit-ups / exclude ST / exclude suspended
  • CSI 300 / CSI 500 / CSI 1000
  • Market-cap weighted / equal weighted

Every option is legitimate and has its reasons, and the combinatorial space is large enough to "tune" significant excess out of any mediocre strategy. Researchers rarely cheat deliberately — the more common path: try a few benchmarks and unconsciously remember the one with good-looking results. This is exactly Lecture 4's "researcher degrees of freedom" recurring at the quantity-definition layer — more hidden than parameter-layer freedom, because it hides under the name of "convention" and never enters the robustness-check checklist.

The institutional countermeasure is isomorphic to factor validation: benchmark conventions go into the pre-registration. The campaign's actual disposition was creating excess_honest (honest-convention excess) as the sole convention for all subsequent reporting, and recomputing every number under the old convention. The naming itself is discipline — making "honest" an explicit attribute rather than a default assumption.

docs.title: 4. Another Mine on the Same Layer: Dividend Double Deduction
docs.text:
The A-share panel's second convention flaw (found in the same period): when constructing the return series, dividends on ex-dividend dates were deducted twice — total returns systematically understated.

The correction formula is clean:

True total return = (1 + panel return) / (f_ratio)²

(f_ratio is the adjustment factor; dividing by f_ratio² exactly cancels the double deduction.) After correction, it aligned with independent tushare data with zero error.

This case's teaching value lies in its conclusion structure:

  • Relative-quantity conclusions survive: relative rankings among factors, the signs of long-short spreads are largely unchanged under overall understatement — because the bias acts nearly proportionally on both sides
  • Absolute-quantity conclusions are all distorted: any "annualized X%" style statement of absolute level is void

Generalized into an audit principle: how much a data bias damages your conclusions depends on whether they rest on differences or levels. Conclusions resting on differences (rankings, spreads, relative strength) are robust to same-direction bias; conclusions resting on levels (returns, volatility, the denominator of Sharpe) are damaged together. Check which kind your key conclusions depend on, and you know how much audit budget to spend on data conventions.

docs.title: 5. Completing the Audit Stack: The Fifth Layer
docs.text:
The Lecture 5 four-layer audit stack can now be completed with the final layer beneath the foundation:

第 5 层  量的定义     基准构成 / 超额的定义 / 可比性     —— 这个量在度量你以为的东西吗
第 4 层  统计充分性   DSR / 多重检验校正
第 3 层  收益来源     正交化 / 归因分解
第 2 层  可实现性     换手 × 成本敏感性
第 1 层  数据地基     复权 / 日期戳 / 拼接               —— 第七讲、第九讲

The fifth layer is the least audited, because when it breaks it throws no error: code runs normally, numbers come out normally, charts look nice. The limit-up-excluding benchmark ran the entire campaign before being exposed in one cross-reconciliation; the dividend double deduction was caught only by a strong check like "zero-error alignment against an independent data source".

Two general countermeasures (proven effective in the campaign):

  1. Independent-source alignment check: align panel returns point-by-point against at least one independent data source; the error should be exactly zero — any non-zero points to a convention difference worth chasing
  2. Convention inventory: list every benchmark construction rule, adjustment method, and exclusion logic as an explicit checklist in the pre-registration document. A convention you cannot write down ("just the default one") is the biggest risk exposure

docs.title: 6. Lecture Summary
docs.text:
• Benchmark excludes limit-ups + strategy holds limit-up stocks + limit-up next-day drift = "excess" requiring no alpha whatsoever; and that excess is unobtainable live (you can't buy limit-up stocks)
  • The benchmark is a high-degree-of-freedom research decision and must enter pre-registration; the "honest convention" should be explicitly named and become the sole reporting convention
  • Dividend double deduction: relative-quantity conclusions survive, absolute-quantity conclusions are distorted — allocate audit budget by whether conclusions depend on differences or levels
  • The audit stack's fifth layer (quantity definition) fails silently; catch it with independent-source alignment and convention inventories

Discussion question: A long-short hedged strategy (long top group + short bottom group, both selected from the same pool) versus a pure long-only index-enhanced strategy — which has higher exposure to the benchmark artifact, and why? (Hint: the long-short "benchmark" is the pool itself; the long-only benchmark is an external index — through which path must the artifact enter returns?)

docs.title: Lecture 9 · Five Pitfalls of the Futures Panel: Walking Chapter 3's Methodology Through a Complete Process
docs.text: Chapter 3 · Hidden Mines in Data Conventions (Lecture 3, chapter finale) Learning objectives: through five real defects of the futures panel, drill the complete convention-audit process of "discover → localize → adjudicate → dispose"; understand the decision criteria for "campaign continues vs stops". Prerequisites: Lectures 7 and 8.

docs.title: 0. Introduction
docs.text:
The previous two lectures each dug into one mine. This lecture switches mode: put the futures panel's five mines on one table, and run each through the same process — symptoms, root cause, impact adjudication, disposition decision. The goal is not to memorize these five pitfalls (change vendors and the pitfalls change) but to drill the standard moves of convention auditing into muscle memory.

The five pitfalls at a glance:

# Pitfall Type Impact surface Campaign decision 1 Double adjustment Return construction error Strategies held across rolls (carry wiped out) Panel rebuilt (detailed in Lecture 7) 2 Night-session date stamp misalignment Timestamp convention Cross-source joins, calendar alignment Returns recomputed by per-instrument row order, campaign continues 3 Roll gaps unhandled Splice artifact False signals for trend/breakout factors Detection tool + factor-layer avoidance 4 $oi coverage erratum Metadata cognition error Explanatory power of factors referencing open interest Cognition corrected, annotation on record 5 End-of-panel overrun Infrastructure boundary Backtest crashes / silent truncation Test window pulled back one trading day

docs.title: 1. Pitfall Two: Night-Session Date Stamp Misalignment — A "Don't Fix the Data" Decision
docs.text:
Symptom: 180 "Sunday" rows mixed into a 918-day panel. By the calendar, futures night sessions belong to the next trading day, but the vendor stamps the data at persistence time by the night session's actual clock time at open — a night session opening Sunday 21:00 gets stamped with Sunday's date.

Root cause: not a data error, but a timestamp convention (the vendor uses clock time, research uses the trading calendar). The two conventions are each internally consistent; only mixing them errs.

Key adjudication: item-by-item checks found — - The return series is correct: each instrument's row order is correct; computing returns by differencing the row order works fine - The misalignment occurs only in cross-source joins: joining this panel's dates against another table stamped by the trading calendar (e.g., the open-interest table) misaligns dates by exactly one day

Disposition: don't fix the data (re-stamping dates risks introducing new errors); change the usage — returns are always computed by per-instrument row order; cross-source joins always run a date-alignment check first. The campaign continued with zero interruption.

This pitfall's teaching point is the audit's "impact adjudication" step: upon finding a convention mismatch, first ask which downstream computations are infected and which are naturally immune, then decide whether to fix the data or change the usage. Blindly rebuilding the panel could turn a harmless convention difference into a real error.

docs.title: 2. Pitfall Three: Roll Gaps — The Boundary Between Artifact and Signal
docs.text:
Symptom and root cause: at the dominant-continuous splice points, if adjustment is incomplete (or the raw spread is deliberately preserved), the roll day produces a price gap. This gap is a splice artifact, not market information — but trend and breakout factors don't distinguish the two: one fake gap = one fake breakout signal = one fake trade.

The layered disposition design: 1. Detection tool: a roll detector — a heuristic scan by open-interest single-day jump (|Δoi| ≥ 30%) or open gap (|gap| ≥ 3%), outputting each instrument's list of roll days 2. Factor-layer avoidance: factors involving breakout logic do not trigger within the roll-day window 3. What we don't do: "repair" the gap itself — trend research sometimes needs exactly the real spread information, and globally smoothing it is over-processing

Teaching point: the correct disposition for an artifact is "identify + isolate", not "exterminate". Over-executing data cleaning is as dangerous as under-executing; the dividing line is "which kind of research treats this feature as noise, and which kind as information".

docs.title: 3. Pitfall Four: The $oi Coverage Erratum — Cognition Errata Are More Common Than Data Errata
docs.text:
Symptom and root cause: research documents long recorded "the open-interest column $oi is missing for some instruments". A systematic check found: full coverage — the earlier "partially missing" was a misreading of one early sampling inspection, written into the documents as fact and propagated.

Damage mechanism: this false belief prematurely ruled out several research directions ("open-interest factors can't be done cross-sectionally across all instruments"), and also gave some factor results a wrong exculpatory explanation ("performance is poor because oi data is missing"). Wrong data can be recomputed and corrected; wrong beliefs about the data silently distort research choices — the latter never appears in any code.

Disposition: cognition correction + documented erratum trail; the wrongly excluded directions re-entered the opportunity list for evaluation.

Teaching point: the objects of audit are not just data, but also data dictionaries / coverage notes / oral consensus. Periodically script-test "the data properties the documents claim" (coverage, start/end dates, null rates); any mismatch between measured and claimed is an erratum candidate.

docs.title: 4. Pitfall Five: End-of-Panel Overrun — Infrastructure Boundaries Need Pre-Registration Discipline Too
docs.text:
Symptom: the qlib backtester reads calendar[i+1] at the final step (settlement needs the T+1 calendar). When the test window's end abuts the panel's last day, it overruns and crashes outright.

Adjudication: this is the tool's hard boundary, not a strategy problem. But its dangerous variant is the silent version: in some environments it doesn't crash but truncates the last segment — the backtest drops a few days, the numbers shift slightly, nobody notices.

Disposition: the convention is that the test window's end stays ≥1 trading day before the panel's last day (written into config defaults after field testing). Teaching point: infrastructure boundary conditions belong in the experiment specification, as explicit as statistical thresholds — "the legal value domain of the backtest window" should also be a section of the pre-registration document.

docs.title: 5. Wrap-Up: The Standard Process of Convention Auditing
docs.text:
With the five pitfalls walked through, extract the common process — Chapter 3's final deliverable:

① 症状     异常数字 / 崩溃 / 交叉对账不一致 / 文档与实测不符
② 根因     数据错误? 约定差异? artifact? 认知错误? 工具边界?
③ 影响面   哪些下游被感染、哪些免疫（差分 vs 水平、行序 vs 日期、
           跨换月 vs 短周期……按第七讲"接触面"原则排优先级）
④ 裁定     修数据 / 改用法 / 隔离 artifact / 修正认知 / 只写规范
⑤ 处置     执行 + 勘误编号留痕 + 历史结论重述（不改历史文档，只限定效力范围）
⑥ 下游     受影响的预注册：功效重估、门槛复核、必要时撤回（第七讲）

And three meta-principles running through Chapter 3:

  1. Audit priority correlates positively, not negatively, with how "plausible" a result is (Lecture 7: being wrong about the good is costly)
  2. Fixing data is the last resort — convention mismatches change the usage, artifacts get isolated, cognition errors get corrected in documents (of Chapter 9's five pitfalls, only double adjustment actually triggered a panel rebuild)
  3. Errata must leave a trail and must not tamper with history — old documents get narrowed annotations, new conclusions get restated per corrected numbers, keeping history forever recomputable (this was the institutional precondition for D-9 to be corrected)

docs.title: 6. Chapter 3 Summary
docs.text:
• The five pitfalls cover five failure types: construction errors, convention mismatches, splice artifacts, cognition errors, tool boundaries
  • The six-step audit process: symptoms → root cause → impact surface → adjudication → disposition → downstream
  • The criterion for "campaign continues vs stops": the correctness of the core return series (after pitfall two's adjudication the campaign continued; pitfall one shook the return foundation, so the panel was rebuilt)
  • Convention auditing is not an entry-level chore but a continuing obligation — four of the five pitfalls were discovered mid-campaign

Chapter 2 built an honest validation institution; Chapter 3 demonstrated that this institution's foundation (data and quantity definitions) itself requires an audit of the same grade. Chapter 4 turns to the final question: after all validation passes, what must a surviving strategy go through before going live — and why "going live" is still not the end.

Discussion question: Pitfall two's (timestamp convention) "don't fix the data, change the usage" decision depends on the discipline that "all downstream switched to computing by row order". If a researcher joining six months later doesn't know this convention and joins an external table by date — what mechanism can guarantee such "conventions" don't get lost with staff turnover? (Hint: compare the failure modes of "written in documents" versus "written into code".)

docs.title: Lecture 10 · funding carry: What a Surviving Strategy Looks Like
docs.text: Chapter 4 · What a Surviving Strategy Looks Like (first lecture) Learning objectives: using the course's only SUPPORTED case as a specimen, understand the distance between "passing validation" and "worth deploying"; master return-source decomposition and magnitude-expectation management. Prerequisites: Chapter 2 (the verdict system), Lecture 7 (the futures version of carry died of double adjustment).

docs.title: 1. The case: crypto perpetual funding-rate carry
docs.text:
Strategy: under the funding-rate mechanism of crypto perpetual contracts, when the rate is positive longs pay shorts, and when negative shorts pay longs. The strategy shorts high-rate instruments (collecting funding) and longs low/negative-rate instruments — returns come from the funding rate itself, with the price legs roughly hedged.

Verdict (pre-registered, one-shot OOS):

SUPPORTed: OOS annualized +2.37%, p < 0.0001. All eight sub-tests (F1–F8) passed.

This is the only all-green verdict since the two chapters of the validation system went live. But the point of this lecture is precisely that all green does not mean the story is over. After the verdict come three questions: where does the money come from, how much is there, and how long will it keep coming.

docs.title: 2. First question: where does the money come from — return-source decomposition
docs.text:
The validation pipeline decomposed the strategy's returns by source:

Funding-rate contribution = 109%.

Translation: the price legs contribute −9% — the strategy loses a little on price, and all of the net return (and more) comes from the accrual of funding fees. This structure is good news: the funding rate is a mechanical cash flow (payment enforced by protocol rules), not a price prediction; a negative price leg means the hedge is slightly overdone, but it decouples the strategy from price direction.

Contrast with the Lesson-5 lesson (the "pseudo alpha" whose 92% of returns were explained by style beta): this 109% is a legitimate return structure: the source is clear, the mechanism is explainable, and its relation to known risk premiums is clean (a carry-type return, in the same family as commodity carry and currency carry). The point of the orthogonalization adversary test here is to confirm "it isn't earning momentum/value/low-vol money" — and source decomposition answers that question more thoroughly.

But note that a deeper question surfaces: if 109% of returns come from funding, this strategy is by nature not a "prediction strategy" but a "fee-collection strategy". It predicts no prices; it simply stands on the receiving side of the funding payment stream. This determines all of its subsequent properties — magnitude, risk, monitoring focus — which are completely different from those of a prediction-type strategy.

docs.title: 3. Second question: how much — magnitude and the "cash-management grade" positioning
docs.text:
Annualized 2.37%. When the fake carry of Lecture 7 claimed 18%, it nearly fooled everyone; this real carry yields only 2.37% — the course returns for the third time to the same law:

Real alpha is small and ugly; fake alpha is big and plausible.

The correct handling of 2.37% is not disappointment but reclassification: this magnitude belongs not to "strategy returns" but to "cash-management enhancement" — it benchmarks against interest income on idle margin, not against the main strategy's return target. The actual positioning decision was made exactly that way: a satellite return stream of the portfolio, occupying a small share of capital, not playing the main-assault role.

Another dimension of magnitude expectation: volatility. The funding rate is regime-dependent — rates run high during bull-market mania (a harvest for the strategy) and hug the ground in quiet periods (returns near zero). 2.37% is the sample-period average; it is not an annuity arriving evenly every month, but feast-or-famine years that follow market sentiment. This property directly determines what the next lecture's shadow monitoring should watch.

docs.title: 4. Third question: how long will it last — pre-designing decay monitoring
docs.text:
The ultimate risk of a fee-collection strategy is that the reason for the fee disappears: the funding-rate mechanism changes, or market participants arbitrage high-rate instruments back to equilibrium (crowding). For this reason, the monitoring plan was pre-registered at the moment of the verdict, not improvised after trouble:

  • Continuous decomposition of return composition: the funding contribution share is the primary monitoring metric — if it starts sliding from 109% (the price legs beginning to dominate), that is an early warning of mechanism decay
  • Rate-regime tracking: the historical percentile of the cross-sectional rate level, to judge whether the current period is feast or famine, rather than misreading a quiet period as "strategy failure"
  • The variant ban: taking effect simultaneously with the verdict — it is forbidden to derive new variants around it (changing the instrument pool, adding leverage, altering hedge ratios) and apply for validation again. The rationale is isomorphic to Lecture 6's hypothesis-family embargo: a variant is a disguised retest of the same OOS data; every variant derived dilutes the statistical power of the original verdict

The variant ban deserves one more sentence because it is counterintuitive: the strategy passed validation, so why not let it "evolve"? Because the choice of evolution direction is guided by impressions from the same dataset — you keep feeling "it would be better if we swapped those two instruments", and that feeling itself comes from memory of in-sample performance. Deriving variants along that feeling means repeatedly overdrawing the same stretch of OOS with in-sample intuition. To genuinely evolve, go forward: new data, new pre-registration.

docs.title: 5. The complete dossier of a strategy
docs.text:
Laid out here is the complete dossier of funding carry, as the standard template of "a surviving strategy":

Dimension Content Hypothesis Mechanical (funding payment stream), non-predictive Verdict Pre-registered one-shot OOS: SUPPORTED (+2.37%/yr, p<0.0001, F1–F8 all passed) Return structure Funding contribution 109%, price legs −9%, decoupled from price direction Positioning Cash-management-grade satellite return stream, not a main strategy Risk profile Rate is regime-dependent (feast-or-famine years); mechanism-change risk; crowding risk Pre-registered monitoring Funding contribution share + rate percentile; decay-trigger conditions written in advance Variant ban In effect; evolution only via forward new pre-registration Next step 30-day shadow monitoring (next lecture)

Contrast with the treatment of those 290 factors in Lecture 5 — not one of them made it to the second row of this table. Passing validation is not the endpoint; it is the starting point of being qualified to be taken seriously.

docs.title: 6. Lecture summary
docs.text:
• Return-source decomposition (109% from funding) is a more thorough "new money vs old money" test than orthogonalization; fee-collection strategies and prediction strategies require completely different risk frameworks
  • The correct positioning of 2.37% annualized is cash-management grade — magnitude-expectation management is an extension of the validation system
  • Decay monitoring is pre-registered at verdict time: watch return composition, not NAV
  • The variant ban: derivative improvements after passing validation are disguised OOS retests; evolution goes forward only

Reflection question: suppose the funding contribution share falls to 60% in some future quarter (the price-leg contribution turns positive), while the strategy's NAV is unchanged. Under this lecture's monitoring logic, is that good news or bad news? (Hint: a rising price-leg contribution means the strategy is drifting from "collecting fees" toward "predicting prices" — its source of risk has changed, and the original SUPPORTED verdict did not cover this form.)

docs.title: Lecture 11 · Shadow Mode: The Last Stretch Before Going Live, and the Truth of Operations
docs.text: Chapter 4 · What a Surviving Strategy Looks Like (second lecture, closing the chapter) Learning objectives: understand the design purpose and monitoring metrics of shadow mode; through a real operational incident, understand the "meta-question of monitoring systems" — monitoring systems break too. Prerequisite: Lecture 10.

docs.title: 1. What shadow mode is: live trading without capital
docs.text:
After funding carry was judged SUPPORTED, it did not go straight to real money; it entered a 30-day frozen monitoring period (shadow mode): the strategy generates signals daily under live-trading logic, computes virtual positions and virtual P&L, and the ledger is logged daily — but no orders are placed.

How it differs from backtesting: shadow mode consumes real data arriving in real time, experiencing genuine data delays, gaps, and out-of-order arrivals; how it differs from live trading: no execution feedback and no capital occupied.

The design purpose has three layers:

  1. Validating the last mile of "implementability": whether the execution assumptions in the backtest (fillable at close price, fees as configured) hold in a real-time environment — only shadow mode can expose this
  2. Validating the runtime environment itself: whether the chain of data pipeline, signal computation, and ledger bookkeeping can run stably for 30 days — many strategies die not of the market but of their own operations
  3. Accumulating forward samples: the 30-day shadow record is a zero-cost, entirely uncontaminated stretch of forward data, citable for the deployment decision

docs.title: 2. The monitoring metric system of shadow mode
docs.text:
The monitoring design for funding carry's shadow period (carrying over Lecture 10's "pre-registered monitoring" principle, written before deployment):

Layer What is monitored Triggered action Data layer Arrival delay, gaps, duplication of market/funding data Degrade and retry; timeout alert Signal layer Deviation of signals from backtest convention Pause signals when deviation exceeds limits; manual review Ledger layer Self-consistency of virtual positions/cash/P&L (every entry reconcilable) On reconciliation failure enter DEGRADED; forbid end-of-day settlement Business layer Return composition (funding vs price legs), consistency with the structure at verdict time Departure from the verdict-time pattern triggers review (the practical version of Lecture 10's reflection question)

The state machine has three tiers: HEALTHY / DEGRADED / HALTED. The key design is degrade before continuing — when the ledger is inconsistent, it is better to stop bookkeeping than to produce "wrong numbers that look normal". This carries on Lecture 3's principle: when a system misbehaves, the most dangerous thing is not downtime but silently producing wrong results.

docs.title: 3. Real incident retrospective: the K2 false positive — the monitoring system fooled you, who monitors it
docs.text:
An event that actually occurred during the shadow period, of extremely high teaching value. The K2 detector (responsible for settlement-booking reconciliation) repeatedly alerted "settlement not booked", pushing the system into DEGRADED and flooding the alert channel. Post-hoc verification: the settlement had in fact been correctly booked — it was the detector's own judgment logic that was flawed (a boundary condition of the reconciliation time window), a false positive.

The same defect pattern recurred twice (after the first fix, it was once misjudged as "passed" — because the retest happened within the detector's time-window threshold since the last alert, the test itself was invalid). Secondary problems exposed along the way:

  • Alert fatigue: false positives flooding at a rate of one every few seconds drowned the visibility of real alerts — the first design principle of an alerting system is tiering (fatal/warning/info); untiered alerts equal no alerts
  • Self-deception of "the retest passed": fix verification must be done on the defect's true time scale (the detector's window is 30 minutes, so verification must wait past the window); a "pass" on a shorter scale has zero validity
  • The reconciliation cost of separating alerts from books: the alert says not booked, the ledger says booked — when two sources conflict, adjudication needs third-party evidence (raw settlement records). An operations system must define in advance "what counts as authoritative when conflicts occur"

The meta-lesson from this event is the core of this lecture:

The monitoring system is part of the system; it breaks too, and it breaks in a more insidious way — when it breaks it does not stop producing output; it only outputs wrong certainty. For every detector of the monitoring system, ask: what does the world look like when the detector itself fails? If the answer is "same as normal" (false negative) or "fires everywhere" (false positive), the detector needs another layer of validation — meta-monitoring, or at least a manual spot-check channel.

docs.title: 4. The economics of shadow mode: when is this apparatus worth building
docs.text:
The cost must be faced honestly: shadow mode is not free — it is a quasi-production system requiring development, operations, and staffing (in this case the shadow chain included daily data pulls, signal computation, ledger, reconciliation, tiered alerting, and a state machine, and there really was an operational incident of data interruption requiring retroactive reconciliation). Is it worth building this for a cash-management-grade strategy yielding 2.37% annualized?

The campaign's actual trade-offs, presented as they were:

  • Scale decides: the strategy's capacity is large (it can carry substantial capital) and its execution frequency is low (daily), so the shadow system can be thin — daily batch processing suffices, no tick-level monitoring needed
  • Verdict and deployment decoupled: shadow mode validates pipeline implementability, not a re-verification of strategy validity (that is the OOS verdict's job). So its exit criterion is not "good shadow-period returns" (30 days of returns carry no statistical significance), but "30 days with zero unexplained ledger discrepancies and zero fatal pipeline failures"
  • Resist the sunk-cost temptation: once the shadow system is built and running smoothly, psychological pressure arises — "we've come this far, let's just go live". The grounds for going live remain only the verdict + pipeline health; the toil of the shadow period constitutes no statistical evidence whatsoever

docs.title: 5. Chapter 4 summary
docs.text:
Lectures 10 and 11 together answer the final link of the entire question chain set up in Chapter 1:

290 factors → zero survivors under validation → the sole survivor at 2.37% annualized, sourced from the funding mechanism → decay monitoring and the variant ban pre-registered at verdict time → 30 days of shadow mode validating the pipeline → only then, the deployment decision.

Two counterintuitive conclusions to remember:

  1. The hardest part is not keeping the strategy alive, but staying humble about "having survived" — magnitude repositioning (cash-management grade), the variant ban, pre-registered monitoring are all institutions that cool down "success". The reason has recurred throughout the course: in this trade, the moments that look most like success are the moments when bias most easily sneaks in (the operations version of Lecture 7's plausibility bias).
  2. The failure mode of a monitoring system is more insidious than a strategy's — it outputs certainty, and keeps outputting even when broken. Meta-monitoring and manual spot-check channels are not redundancy; they are necessities.

Chapter 5 (the final chapter) rises from the individual strategy back to the research organization: how opportunities are screened, how directions get cut, how negative results are recorded — gathering the whole course's methodology into a set of research discipline you can take with you.

Reflection question: after 30 days of failure-free shadow mode, someone proposes: "the shadow system is built anyway; let's hook up two other unvalidated strategies to run in shadow alongside, at no extra cost." What hidden costs does this proposal have? (Hint: on which decision will the shadow-run data be used? For those two strategies' validation — OOS consumption, multiple testing — does the shadow period count as one "peek"?)
