docs.title: Lecture 12 · The Discipline of Opportunity Screening: Before Diving In
docs.text: Chapter 5 · Distilling the Method (first lecture) Learning objectives: master the ex-ante screening framework for research directions — orthogonal discrimination, exclusion rules, opportunity-cost accounting; understand the "research ledger" as organizational memory. Prerequisite: the whole course (this chapter gathers the methodology of multiple campaign threads).

docs.title: 1. The problem: the bottleneck of research capacity is not ideas
docs.text:
After running a complete "factory + validation + shadow" system, you quickly discover the true constraint structure:

  • Ideas are not scarce: ten "can this data make a factor" thoughts pop up every day
  • What is scarce is validation capacity: every OOS window is a one-shot consumable; every piece of engineering investment (data procurement, panel construction, pipeline development) is real cost
  • The most expensive thing is a wrong direction: three weeks sunk into a wrong direction loses not three weeks, but the correct directions that could not be validated during those three weeks

So the form of the question is not "what research to find" but "by what rules to exclude research at the entrance". This lecture's content comes from the opportunity-screening institution gradually solidified in real campaigns.

docs.title: 2. The first gate: the exclusion list (DO NOT RESEARCH)
docs.text:
More important than "what is worth researching" is a written-down "what we no longer research". The real exclusion list (excerpted; behind every entry is a real cost):

  • Falsified hypothesis families: the z-fade spread-reversion family (all three sub-types show no reversion), the earnings-forecast event window (OOS direction reversed), the H1 dispersion Gate (opposite direction) — the same hypothesis family in a different disguise is not a new hypothesis
  • Data unobtainable: the futures-options direction (source blocked, DATA_BLOCKED) — confirm the data first, then talk design
  • Already covered by existing assets: directions whose return sources overlap heavily with validated strategies (the orthogonality requirement, see next section)
  • Exposure-timing types (marked DO NOT RESEARCH YET): not never-do, but under the current evidence structure (style beta explains nearly all excess) there is no testable hypothesis — wait first, don't spin idle

The everyday value of this list is defensive: three months later you yourself will have forgotten why a direction was abandoned, and you will invest in it again — the exclusion list is written for your future self. The "YET" suffix design also matters: it distinguishes "falsified" (evidence against) from "shelved" (currently untestable); the two carry different implications for resource discipline, and mixing them would permanently bury revivable directions.

docs.title: 3. The second gate: orthogonal discrimination — four questions, each a veto
docs.text:
A new opportunity must pass four questions; failing any one knocks it out (a real institution, all four with veto power):

① Is the money it earns already being earned by existing strategies? (return orthogonality) A new opportunity must show its return source is not shared with deployed/validated strategies. funding carry got greenlit because it answered this first question cleanly: funding cash flow, entirely distinct from price prediction.

② Is the data it depends on something others can also easily obtain? (an honest assessment of data moats) If the answer is "everyone has it", then excess can only come from processing quality — which requires a concrete answer to "is my processing really better than others'", not "I feel we're more careful".

③ Can its hypothesis be falsified? (testability) The entrance version of Lecture 3's "a mechanism that can explain any result is no mechanism": before entering research, write down "what result would make me admit it's wrong". If you can't write it, you don't enter.

④ Can you afford the cost of validating it? (power budget) The entrance version of Lecture 7's "power retraction": roughly compute statistical power from expected effect magnitude and available data volume — a direction with insufficient power (say, testing a 3%-magnitude effect over a 350-day window) is formalism no matter how beautiful the design. Not every good idea is worth doing now.

Together, the four questions are four faces of one question: can this opportunity's "truth" be known at an affordable cost?

docs.title: 4. The third gate: the economic investment threshold
docs.text: Opportunities passing the first two gates must also pass an economic accounting: data cost + engineering cost + validation-window consumption, set against "the expected economic value if validation passes" (a prior of magnitude × capacity × survival probability). This is not precise calculation but order-of-magnitude ranking — the purpose is to stop "technically interesting, economically meaningless" projects from crowding out capacity (both research organizations and researchers are naturally drawn to "interesting"; this gate forces "worth it" back in).

docs.title: 5. The research ledger: archiving the screening process itself
docs.text:
The rulings of all the gates above — passed, excluded, shelved — are recorded together with their reasons in the research ledger (a persistent document organized by campaign). Its three functions:

  1. Prevent recurrence: exclusion rules only hold back your future self if written down (Section 2, above)
  2. Locking in re-review trigger conditions: shelved entries carry "what change triggers re-evaluation" (e.g. "re-evaluate line D when options data becomes available in 2026-12"), giving "waiting" an exit rather than oblivion
  3. Booking negative results: the complete record of every REJECTED/INCONCLUSIVE (hypothesis, verdict, numbers, disposition) is an asset — it prevents the same OOS window from being retested in disguise (the enforcement vehicle of Lecture 6's hypothesis-family embargo), and serves as prior evidence for similar future hypotheses

The underlying logic of ledger discipline carries on Lecture 3: do not tamper with history; make history recomputable. A research organization's memory that exists only in individual heads is no memory at all.

docs.title: 6. A complete screening example: how three surviving lines came to be
docs.text:
The direction review after the second round of the futures campaign (the six-direction matrix) ran these gates for real, and the result structure clearly shows how the gates work:

Direction Gate ruling Reason A cross-sectional factors Greenlit Return source orthogonal to existing lines; additional methodological value as the control baseline for the LLM factory B time-series CTA Greenlit Different return source from cross-sectional; time-series convention already in place C spread reversion (z-fade family) Excluded Inherits the prior REJECTED — the first gate intercepts it outright D options Shelved (DATA_BLOCKED) Data unobtainable; re-review trigger condition registered E event type Excluded Overlaps a falsified family F basis / term structure Partially shelved (PARTIAL) Effect magnitude in doubt after D-9; watch line

Note C and E: they were not "reviewed out" — they were instantly killed by the list, which is exactly the point of the first gate: turning the most expensive mistake (redoing what was falsified) into the cheapest ruling.

docs.title: 7. Lecture summary
docs.text:
• The true bottleneck of research capacity is validation resources and direction choice; the essence of a screening institution is protecting expensive investment with cheap vetoes
  • Three gates: exclusion list (with the YET mechanism) → four orthogonality questions (veto power) → economic investment threshold
  • The common core of the four questions: "can this opportunity's 'truth' be known at an affordable cost"
  • The research ledger: rulings archived, re-review conditions locked in, negative results booked — the institutionalization of organizational memory
  • The six-direction matrix example: falsified families killed instantly at the first gate is the highest cost-effectiveness moment of the whole system

Reflection question: someone proposes researching "AI sentiment indicators for A-share market timing". Run it through the four orthogonality questions: which question is most likely to stop it? Which is hardest to answer? (Hint: how do you write falsification conditions for a timing hypothesis — beyond "significantly improves Sharpe", can you state in advance what result counts as failure?)

docs.title: Lecture 13 · The Course Concludes: The Complete Puzzle of Research Discipline Through One Campaign
docs.text: Chapter 5 · Distilling the Method (second lecture, the course finale) Learning objectives: assemble the twelve lectures' concepts into one complete battle map; distill a list of research discipline you can take with you.

docs.title: 1. The course's narrative thread, revisited
docs.text:
Thirteen stories were told, but there is only one thread: when AI drives the cost of "generating hypotheses" to nearly zero, the center of value of the research system shifts wholesale to what comes after hypothesis generation.

第一章  工厂很能干        290 个因子一晚上，代码质量过硬，假设质量平平
第二章  但成绩单不可信    多重检验 + 风格 beta + 净费 + ——独立验证零存活
第三章  连地基都要审      双重复权 + 基准伪影 + 五坑——数据与量定义的审计
第四章  幸存者依然谦卑    +2.37%/yr，现金管理级，判决只是获得认真对待的资格
第五章  瓶颈回到选择      排除清单 + 正交四问 + 经济门槛——便宜的否决保护昂贵的投入

The numerical version of the thread (worth memorizing):

Best self-reported +26.5% → independent validation 0 survivors; the fake carry +18% (adjustment bug) → the real carry +2.37%; REJECTED −0.49% / INCONCLUSIVE +1.00% (p=0.062) / SUPPORTED +2.37%. Real alpha is small and ugly; fake alpha is big and plausible.

docs.title: 2. A battle map: components and interfaces of the full system
docs.text:
┌─ 机会筛选 ──────────────────────────────────────────────┐
│  排除清单(DO NOT RESEARCH / YET) → 正交四问 → 经济门槛    │
│         ↓ 通过                                          │
├─ 工厂层（AI）───────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  数据面板(人定) → 五步循环 → 候选假设流                   │
│         ↓ 产出单位=候选假设,不是可上线因子                 │
├─ 验证层（制度）─────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  独立数据复算 → 预注册门槛(DSR/主副裁判/分年/正交化)       │
│  → OOS 一次性判定 → 三种判决(S/R/I) → 假设族封禁          │
│         ↓ SUPPORTED                                     │
├─ 地基审计（贯穿）───────────────────────────────────────┤
│  五层审计栈: 量的定义→数据地基→可实现性→收益来源→统计充分  │
│  口径审计六步: 症状→根因→影响面→裁定→处置→下游             │
│         ↓                                               │
├─ 部署层 ───────────────────────────────────────────────┤
│  影子模式30天(链路验证) → 部署决策 → 监控预注册(衰减+变体禁令)│
│         ↓ 全程                                          │
└─ 记忆层 ───────────────────────────────────────────────┐
   研究账本: 裁决留档/负结果入账/勘误编号/历史可复算          │

No individual component is new — pre-registration has been the clinical-trials standard for decades, multiple-testing correction is common knowledge in academic statistics, and shadow mode is the canary release of software engineering. The novelty of this system lies only in the consistency of its seriousness: when hypothesis production is accelerated a hundredfold by AI, the enforcement intensity of these old institutions must scale in step, or they degrade from "line of defense" into "decoration".

docs.title: 3. Ten rules of research discipline to take with you
docs.text:
The whole course compressed into ten, each annotated with its source lecture:

  1. On leaderboards, read the number-of-evaluations column before the returns column — combos/versions cap the luck component (E2)
  2. Ask three questions of every result: what's the benchmark, were costs counted, how many times was it tested (E2)
  3. Excess returns don't distinguish new money from old money; orthogonalization and source decomposition do — "alpha" that is 92% style-explained is not alpha (E3/E5/E10)
  4. Pre-registration is finished before touching the data; a rule change = redoing the experiment (E4)
  5. OOS is a consumable: one-shot verdicts, hypothesis-family embargoes, variant bans — all point to the same principle (E4/E6/E10)
  6. Audit the most expected-looking numbers first — being wrong in a flattering way is costly (E7)
  7. Fixing data is the last resort: change usage by convention, isolate artifacts, fix the documentation when the cognition was wrong (E9)
  8. Whether a conclusion depends on differences or levels determines its immunity class to data defects (E8)
  9. Monitoring breaks too, and keeps outputting certainty when broken — meta-monitoring and manual spot checks are necessities (E11)
  10. Write "what not to research" as formally as "what to research" (E12)

docs.title: 4. The campaign-matrix endgame and "the compounding of negative results"
docs.text:
The panorama of the real campaigns as of this course's writing (simplified):

Campaign Ending Legacy A-shares Zero excess under the honest convention, DSR all FAIL the excess_honest convention, the validation institution, a complete specimen of fake alpha Futures r1 136 trials, postloop all FAIL the pre-registered validation pipeline itself, three of the five traps Futures r2 In progress (matrix system) six-direction screening, the D-9 erratum, L2 → watch line crypto r1 Top spot +10.85% not robust, actually a baseline empirical proof that "leaderboard top ≠ real signal" crypto r2 Real signals = vol_20d/reversal_5d (textbook factors) the reasonable expectation for the loop: rediscovering the classics, not inventing novelty funding carry SUPPORTED +2.37%/yr, in shadow the sole survivor, the pre-registered monitoring template Index rebalancing INCONCLUSIVE, moved to a forward round "waiting" is also a verdict Earnings forecasts REJECTED the template for the verdict-execution three-piece set

Note the composition of the "Legacy" column: almost no legacy is a positive-return strategy; nearly all are institutions, conventions, templates, and specimens. This is not consolation — it is the real asset structure of this kind of research organization. Strategies decay; discipline compounds. A losing campaign that produced "a validation institution + erratum capability + an exclusion list" is far richer than a campaign that made money on unaudited conventions without knowing why. The latter's problem: its profits cannot be attributed, hence cannot be replicated, and no one knows when they will vanish.

The compounding of negative results is the idea this course most wants to leave behind: record every REJECTED as a recomputable page in the archive, and your research system grows; forget them, and you are just paying the same tuition over and over.

docs.title: 5. Closing: the researcher's place in the AI era
docs.text:
Back to the sentence at the end of Lecture 1 — the full version can now be given:

What the AI factor factory replaces is the "hands". But "judgment" — is the data trustworthy, is the convention honest, do the results warrant the selection base, is this direction worth a window — is not only not replaced; its scarcity is amplified a hundredfold, because the supply of hypotheses is amplified a hundredfold.

Everything in this course is, in essence, thirteen facets of one thing: in an era of hypothesis surplus, the researcher's core skill migrates from "having good ideas" to "cheaply killing bad ideas". The factory produces cheaply; you veto cheaply — both ends of the system are "cheap", and what is saved in the middle are the years no longer spent paying real money for noise.

Closing reflection question (no next lecture to collect answers; answer it yourself): suppose tomorrow a stronger model appears and the factory's hypothesis quality rises to researcher level. Which lectures of this course will become obsolete, and which will not? Why? (One line of thought: what becomes obsolete is descriptive content about "the boundary of AI capability"; what doesn't is institutional content about "validation and selection" — the former depreciates with technology, the latter appreciates with the supply of hypotheses.)

docs.title: Extra 1 · The Two Crypto Campaigns: The Triple Persona of a Leaderboard Top
docs.text: Extras (independent of the mainline order, but Lectures 2 and 5 are recommended reading first) Learning objective: through the complete story of the two crypto campaigns, demonstrate the three faces of "the same number" under three kinds of scrutiny.

docs.title: 1. Case overview
docs.text:
The crypto campaign ran two rounds. The first round's leaderboard top: +10.85% — a number exciting enough for anyone. The final conclusion: not robust; the top was a pure baseline. The real signals confirmed after restarting validation in the second round: vol_20d (20-day volatility) and reversal_5d (5-day reversal).

The value of this extra lies in this: the number +10.85% never changed from start to finish; what changed was the lens looking at it. The same number showed three faces under triple scrutiny.

docs.title: 2. The first face: the star on the leaderboard
docs.text: Looked at in isolation: +10.85%, self-consistent strategy logic, a beautiful backtest curve. This is its most dangerous moment — Lecture 5 said that a human's default logic for checking numbers is "audit the absurd, wave through the plausible", and 10.85% is a "believably restrained" number for crypto (two orders of magnitude below the 100% scams, one order above the boring 2%). A textbook case of the plausibility bias (Lecture 7).

docs.title: 3. The second face: a baseline under forensic examination
docs.text:
The first layer of dissection: the two top factors on the leaderboard (9ebd7fdc / cfa700d4) were identified as pure baselines — the code audit found their "factor logic" was actually a degenerate form: equivalent to holding the equal-weight benchmark, or applying an uninformative ranking across all instruments. Their +10.85% was not alpha but the beta of the market itself over that period.

The teaching point of this layer is "how it was found": not by statistics (statistically it looked great), but by reading the code. Auditing the factor-implementation layer is the most easily skipped link of the validation pipeline — everyone assumes "the code that produced the numbers is the code it claims to be". LLM-generated factors need this checkpoint all the more: Lecture 2 noted the versions column holds 33 versions — each additional version adds a further burden of proof that "the code is still doing what it claims".

docs.title: 4. The third face: the survivors under the honest convention
docs.text:
Re-validated after stripping the fake top: the only real signals left are vol_20d and reversal_5d. Lecture 3's conclusion two receives its cleanest empirical proof here: after two full rounds of the loop and hundreds of factors, the two survivors are both textbook factors — the volatility effect and short-term reversal are phenomena validated for decades in cross-sectional research.

The corollary deserves its own line: the reasonable expectation of an AI loop is "efficiently rediscovering the classics", not "inventing novelty". If you hired a research assistant and after a year his conclusion was "momentum and reversal also work in crypto" — would you think the year was worth it? In the new world of near-zero hypothesis cost, the answer is yes: he ruled out everything else, and exclusion is itself output (Lecture 5's "compounding of negative results").

docs.title: 5. Extra summary
docs.text:
• The three faces of +10.85%: leaderboard star → baseline under code audit → noise after stripping
  • The factor-implementation audit (reading the code) cannot be skipped; statistical testing cannot cover "the code doesn't do what it claims"
  • The reasonable output expectation of loop mining: rediscover the classics + exclude the rest

Reflection question: in what market environment is a baseline masquerading as a factor most likely to reach the top of a leaderboard? (Hint: periods of high equal-weight-benchmark returns — bull markets. Then can "leaderboard tops clustering in a certain period" itself serve as an audit clue?)

docs.title: Extra 2 · The HITL Reconnaissance Screen: Another Way of Putting the Human in the Loop
docs.text: Extras (Lectures 6 and 12 recommended reading first) Learning objective: understand the design logic of the Human-In-The-Loop (HITL) reconnaissance mode, and its complementary relationship with the fully automated loop.

docs.title: 1. Background: why a "screen filled in by humans"
docs.text:
The main course's full pipeline (factory → validation → shadow) has an implicit scope of applicability: the hypothesis can be fully formalized and backtested on historical data. But one class of opportunities fails this premise:

  • The signals are unstructured (qualitative judgments on news, announcements, rumors)
  • Low frequency (only a few dozen effective events a year); the historical sample is too small to backtest
  • The judgment itself depends on human contextual understanding and can hardly be written as rules in advance

For such opportunities, forcing them into a backtest framework is cutting the foot to fit the shoe; abandoning them is a waste. The third option: a reconnaissance screen — the system scans and records; the human judges and fills in; the judgments settle into forward data.

docs.title: 2. Design: freeze first
docs.text:
Key design decisions of the HITL scanner as actually deployed (online 2026-09-27, verdict date 2026-12-26):

① Pre-registration discipline applies equally. The verdict metrics (precision ≥ 30%, fill rate ≥ 50%) and the verdict date were frozen before going live — Lecture 12's gate institution applied verbatim. The human-in-the-loop is not a discipline-exemption zone: precisely because humans participate, the temptation to "just tweak the standard a bit" is greater.

② Human judgment is structured. The entry interface accepts only discrete fields (direction, confidence tier, reason code), not free-text scoring — guaranteeing the data is statistically analyzable after 90 days. Freestyle judgment cannot be aggregated.

③ The verdict date covers a real event round. The screen monitors index-rebalance events, and the verdict date is set after the 2026-12 rebalance round — so that the verdict happens after "the screen has seen at least one complete round of real events", rather than merely accumulating calendar days.

④ 90 days of observation, no peeking at results midway. Isomorphic to the one-shot OOS verdict: peek midway → learn which signal types perform well → unconsciously change entry behavior → data contaminated. With a human in the loop, the human is the biggest source of degrees of freedom, so the lock must be even tighter.

docs.title: 3. The division of labor between HITL and the fully automated loop
docs.text:
Fully automated loop HITL reconnaissance screen Hypothesis form Formalizable, backtestable Qualitative, low-frequency, context-dependent Human's role Sets panel/convention/thresholds Judges inside the loop Data output Historical backtests A forward-accumulating structured stream of judgments Verdict Pre-registered one-shot OOS verdict Pre-registered metrics + frozen verdict date Main risk Multiple testing Human behavioral drift contaminating the data

What the two share is not technology but the discipline skeleton: frozen criteria, accumulating forward data, a one-shot verdict. The only difference is where the data comes from (backtests vs the stream of human judgments).

docs.title: 4. Extra summary
docs.text:
• HITL's zone of applicability: opportunities that cannot be formalized for backtesting, are low-frequency, and context-dependent
  • Structured entry + frozen criteria + coverage of a complete event round + no peeking midway — this four-piece set locks the human's degrees of freedom within what data quality allows
  • Fully automated and HITL are two data sources of the same validation discipline

Reflection question: why is "fill rate ≥ 50%" among the verdict metrics a necessary condition? (Hint: if only 10% of signals get a filled-in judgment, however high the precision, what is the screen's value as a data asset? — selective entry is itself a form of post-hoc selection bias.)
